bibl.title: Learning to schedule job-shop problems: representation and policy learning using graph neural network and reinforcement learning

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: We propose a framework to learn to schedule a job-shop problem (JSSP) using a graph neural network (GNN) and reinforcement learning (RL).

span.label: job-shop scheduling
span.quote: The job shop scheduling problem (JSSP) is, a type of scheduling problem that aims to determine the optimal sequential assignments of machines to multiple jobs consisting of series of operations while preserving the problem constraints (processing precedence and machine-sharing).

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: In this paper, we propose a framework to construct the scheduling policy for JSSPs using GNN and RL.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because the embedding layer works through pairwise interaction functions that are shared across all node pairs rather than tied to a fixed graph size, the same trained network can be run on graphs with different node counts and edge patterns, which is what carries the policy to unseen instance sizes
span.quote: Due to the pair-wise interaction module, a trained GNN can be applied to the news graphs whose structures (the number of nodes in graph and the edge connectivities) are different from the graphs used for training.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Training on a graph representation forces the policy to key on the structural regularities common to all job shops instead of memorising one instance, which is why it transfers with no further training
span.quote: The scheduling policy learns to consider the inherent structure of the JSSP, rather than learning the characteristics of a specific JSSP instance.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The learned policy beats fixed rules because it re-weights which state features matter at each decision, whereas a dispatching rule always consults the same predetermined features
span.quote: The key advantages of the RL-based approach over the PDR and CDR are that it learns how to adaptively utilize various state features in determining the optimal scheduling actions, while PDRs and CDRs constantly use the predetermined same state features in making the next scheduling actions.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The dense waiting-job reward is used instead of makespan because a reward delivered only at episode end leaves the algorithm unable to assign credit to individual dispatching actions
span.quote: On the other hand, the makespan reward will be realized once only when the given instance is finished; as a result, the RL algorithm has difficulty in assigning credit to the actions in the episode during training.

span.label: Computation time for node embeddings grows rapidly (quadratically in the number of jobs) with instance size.
span.quote: Although the proposed GNN scheduler showed reliable performance on our testing set and benchmark JSSP instances, the computational time to compute the node embeddings rapidly increases as the size of JSSP increases.

span.label: The MDP formulation omits practical shop-floor constraints such as batching, waiting-time regulations and flexible setups.
span.quote: Lastly, the current formulation does not consider more practical constraints such as batch processes and waiting time regulations and flexible shop setup.

span.label: The distribution used to generate training and test instances does not cover real-world job shops.
span.quote: In a practical sense, the distribution P0(g0) used to generate the training and test JSSP instances is not general enough to cover real-world JSSPs.

span.label: The comparison with prior RL schedulers could only test limited generalisation, because those baselines require train and test instances of the same size.
span.quote: Therefore, only a limited generalization test could be conducted for the case where the conjunctive constraints and processing times are different from the training and test data sets.

span.label: The learned scheduler is slower at inference than simple priority dispatching rules.
span.quote: As shown in Figure 8, the proposed GNN-scheduler requires more computational time than PDRs.

span.label: The headline comparison is scoped to instances drawn from the training distribution, and the comparison against the other learned schedulers is scoped by a restriction on testing instances.
span.quote: The proposed GNN scheduler outperformed all PDRs when testing on JSSP instances generated by the distribution used for generating training instances. The proposed GNN scheduler showed robust performances on various sets of benchmark instances in contrast to PDRs, whose solution qualities fluctuated depending on the properties of the given JSSP. Also, the proposed GNN scheduler achieved better scheduling than the RL-based schedulers with the restriction on testing instances.

span.label: The method's cost grows with problem size by the authors' own analysis, which is the quantity a scheduling practitioner would care about.
span.quote: the computational time to compute the node embeddings rapidly increases as the size of JSSP increases

span.label: The reference against which solution quality is judged is another solver's output, not a proven optimum supplied independently.
span.quote: We prepare the validation instances generated through p0(G0). The optimal solutions (minimum makespan) of the validation instances are computed through the Google OR tool

span.label: Training stops on a convergence criterion measured on the validation set, so the reported model is the one that stopped improving on that set.
span.quote: We terminate the training procedure when the makespan of the validation set converges.

span.label: The architecture search behind the reported hyperparameters is reported only as a negative result, with no numbers attached.
span.quote: We tested deeper and thicker ReLU networks while finding the best hyperparameters. The deep and thick ReLU networks than the specified hyperparameter setup did not improve scheduling performance.

span.label: The size-agnostic transferability of graph neural networks, demonstrated in robot control, wind power estimation and weather prediction, is imported into production scheduling to make a scheduler that works on unseen shop sizes
span.quote: We utilize such transferability of GNNs to accomplish the transferable property in our JSSP scheduler.

span.label: Proximal Policy Optimization, a policy-gradient algorithm from the RL literature, is adopted to train the representation and dispatching modules of a job-shop scheduler end to end
span.quote: We use proximal policy optimization (PPO) [37] algorithm, a variant of policy-based RL, to train the GNN based state representation module and the parameterized decision-making policy jointly.

span.label: job shop scheduling problem
span.quote: The job shop scheduling problem (JSSP) is, a type of scheduling problem that aims to determine the optimal sequential assignments of machines to multiple jobs consisting of series of operations while preserving the problem constraints

span.label: MDP
span.quote: We formulate a scheduling process of a JSSP instance as an MDP.

span.label: makespan
span.quote: We aim to learn a scheduling policy that minimizes the makespan Cmax. Cmax is the maximum completion time among jobs, i.e., the total length of the schedule

span.label: priority dispatching rules
span.quote: These methods mainly include neighborhood search methods and priority dispatching rules

span.label: generalization - AS THE ABSTRACT CLAIMS IT: a superb capability, asserted without a scope
span.quote: We empirically demonstrate that the GNN scheduler, due to its superb generalization capability, outperforms practically favored dispatching rules and RL-based schedulers on various benchmark JSSP.

span.label: generalization - AS THE CONCLUSION SCOPES IT: trained on only small JSSPs and producing high-quality schedules for large ones, with the PDR comparison run on the training distribution
span.quote: Overall, the results demonstrate that our framework can produce a generalizable scheduling policy so that the GNN scheduler trained on only small JSSPs can generate high-quality schedules for large-sized JSSPs without additional training.

span.label: scheduling quality - operationalised entirely as makespan: the maximum completion time among jobs, which is the single quantity the reward function is built to minimise
span.quote: We aim to learn a scheduling policy that minimizes the makespan Cmax. Cmax is the maximum completion time among jobs, i.e., the total length of the schedule

span.label: builds-on → Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., cited as [37]/[38])
span.quote: We use proximal policy optimization (PPO) [37] algorithm, a variant of policy-based RL, to train the GNN based state representation module and the parameterized decision-making policy jointly.

span.label: extends → MARL [10] and MDQN [24] RL-based JSSP schedulers
span.quote: To mimic the experimental procedures reported in [10] and [24], we trained the three GNN schedulers (GNN1, GNN2, and GNN3) with the training JSSP instances with sizes 5×15, 10×10 and 15×20, respectively.

span.label: job shop scheduling problem —operationalised-as→ MDP
span.quote: We formulate a scheduling process of a JSSP instance as an MDP.

span.label: regression (polynomial curve fitting)
span.quote: As the fitted second-order polynomial curve y = 0.0125n2 − 0.1857n + 0.7543 with R2 = 0.9984 represents, the computational time is likely proportional to the square of the number of jobs.

span.label: coefficient of determination
span.quote: Also, as the fitted first-order polynomial curve y = 4.2857m − 21.598 with R2 = 0.9815

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: We randomly generate 20 JSSP instances of each size and solves the problems with the proposed method to estimate the mean and standard deviation of computation times.

span.label: error bars (one standard deviation)
span.quote: The vertical error bars indicate one standard deviation of errors (the statistics are computed from 100 simulations).

span.label: mean
span.quote: The trained GNN scheduler achieved 14.7% average relative error on the test instances.

span.label: On test instances drawn from the training distribution, the trained graph-neural-network scheduler beat every priority dispatching rule tested, reaching 14.7% average relative error against the optimum makespan while all rules other than MOR exceeded 20%.
span.quote: The trained GNN scheduler achieved 14.7% average relative error on the test instances.

span.label: Applied without retraining to published benchmark sets, the scheduler produced average relative errors between 12.6% and 20.9%, the lowest of all methods on every benchmark family except ABZ and TA.
span.quote: The GNN scheduler yielded quality solutions whose average relative errors ranged from 12.6% to 20.9%.

span.label: A scheduler trained only on small randomly generated instances transfers to much larger instances, since the gap between the generically trained GNN0 and the size-matched GNN1-3 was small.
span.quote: Based on the observation that the performance gaps between GNN0 and GNNi (i ∈ 1, 2, 3) are small, we can conclude that the node embedding scheme learned from small sized JSSPs can be generalized to solve large-sized JSSPs.

span.label: Unlike the dispatching rules, whose solution quality swung with the properties of the instance family (MOR and FIFO collapsed on the SWV benchmarks), the GNN scheduler stayed consistently good across instance types.
span.quote: In contrast, our GNN scheduler reliably generated the high-quality scheduling solutions for various types of JSSPs.

span.label: Measured runtime grows roughly with the square of the number of jobs and roughly linearly with the number of machines, matching the n^2 + nm growth in the number of graph edges.
span.quote: As the fitted second-order polynomial curve y = 0.0125n2 − 0.1857n + 0.7543 with R2 = 0.9984 represents, the computational time is likely proportional to the square of the number of jobs.

span.label: Stacking more than three embedding layers bought no measurable scheduling improvement while costing extra computation, so the message-passing depth was fixed at three.
span.quote: However, we experimentally confirmed that K larger than three does not significantly improve the GNN scheduler’s scheduling performance but only requires more computations.

span.label: The learned scheduler pays for its quality in runtime: it is slower than the dispatching rules because it must compute node embeddings before each dispatch, whereas the rules compute no features.
span.quote: As shown in Figure 8, the proposed GNN-scheduler requires more computational time than PDRs.

span.label: Fewer than 20 episodes per parameter update left the state-value estimate with large variance, while more than 20 added no performance, fixing the batch size at 20 episodes.
span.quote: From a series of experiments, we have observed that when n is less than 20, the computed state value has a large variance, while when n is over 20, the performance gain is not significant.

span.label: job shop scheduling problem (JSSP)
span.quote: The job shop scheduling problem (JSSP) is, a type of scheduling problem that aims to determine the optimal sequential assignments of machines to multiple jobs consisting of series of operations while preserving the problem constraints (processing precedence and machine-sharing).

span.label: priority dispatching rule (PDR)
span.quote: A PDR is a heuristic rule that assigns jobs to machines based on their priorities while considering the current status of the system.

span.label: graph state for the JSSP
span.quote: We refer to the conjunctive graph with the node features as the graph state for the JSSP.

span.label: non-trivial state
span.quote: We first define the non-trivial states as the states when (1) at least one machine is available and (2) a machine has strictly more than one operation ready to be processed.

span.label: primitive transition
span.quote: For brevity, we will refer to the original transitions as primitive transitions and non-trivial states as states.

span.label: graph neural network (GNN)
span.quote: A GNN is a type of neural network that takes a graph as input and typically produces an updated graph whose node (or edge) features are embedded with the consideration of edge connectivities and neighborhood node features.

span.label: makespan (Cmax)
span.quote: Cmax is the maximum completion time among jobs, i.e., the total length of the schedule (Cmax = maxj∈J Cj).

span.label: number of jobs (n)
span.quote: We conduct two folds of experiments: (1) fixing m and varying n, (2) varying m, and fixing n.

span.label: number of machines (m)
span.quote: We conduct two folds of experiments: (1) fixing m and varying n, (2) varying m, and fixing n.

span.label: scheduling method (GNN scheduler versus priority dispatching rules)
span.term: scheduling method (GNN scheduler versus priority dispatching rules)
span.quote: For all three experiments, we used various PDRs to compare the performance of the proposed method.

span.label: relative scheduling error (makespan against the optimum)
span.term: relative scheduling error (makespan against the optimum)
span.quote: We evaluated the scheduling performance of a scheduler for a JSSP instance by computing the relative scheduling error defined as follows:

span.label: computation time
span.quote: We randomly generate 20 JSSP instances of each size and solves the problems with the proposed method to estimate the mean and standard deviation of computation times.

span.label: additional training on the test instances (held at zero, zero-shot setting)
span.term: additional training on the test instances (held at zero, zero-shot setting)
span.quote: The experiments were done with the GNN scheduler that is pre-trained as described in section 5 without additional training, i.e., zero-shot setting, as illustrated in Figure 4.

span.label: PPO hyperparameters (learning rate, GAE parameter, clipping parameter, value and entropy coefficients)
span.term: PPO hyperparameters (learning rate, GAE parameter, clipping parameter, value and entropy coefficients)
span.quote: For the learning rate η, GAE parameter λ, clipping parameter (cid:15), value function coefficient α, and entropy bonus coefficient β, we used the same values suggested by [16].

span.label: discount factor gamma
span.quote: We set γ as 1.0 since the target JSSP problem is formulated as a finite MDP.

span.label: 14.7% — average relative makespan error of the trained scheduler on the 100 in-distribution test instances
span.quote: The trained GNN scheduler achieved 14.7% average relative error on the test instances.

span.label: over 20% — average relative error of every dispatching rule except MOR on the same test set
span.quote: The relative scheduling errors of the other PDRs were all over 20%.

span.label: 12.6% to 20.9% — range of the scheduler's average relative error across the published benchmark families
span.quote: The GNN scheduler yielded quality solutions whose average relative errors ranged from 12.6% to 20.9%.

span.label: 4.4% and 2.7% — the two cases where the scheduler was second-best by instance size (20x30 and 20x50), and by how much it trailed the best rule
span.quote: Our scheduler ranked best in all but two size of instances, where it ranked second for the cases of 20×30 and 20×50, with 4.4% and 2.7% gaps in relative error from the best PDR, respectively.

span.label: R2 = 0.9984 — fit quality of the quadratic model relating runtime to the number of jobs
span.quote: As the fitted second-order polynomial curve y = 0.0125n2 − 0.1857n + 0.7543 with R2 = 0.9984 represents, the computational time is likely proportional to the square of the number of jobs.

span.label: R2 = 0.9815 — fit quality of the linear model relating runtime to the number of machines
span.quote: Also, as the fitted first-order polynomial curve y = 4.2857m − 21.598 with R2 = 0.9815

span.label: K = 3 — number of stacked embedding layers (hops of message passing) used in the GNN
span.quote: We set the number of embedding iterations as K = 3.

span.label: 100 — number of held-out test instances sampled from the training distribution
span.quote: We measured the performances of the trained GNN scheduler and PDRs over the 100 testing instances sampled from P0(G0), which were used to generate training instances.

span.label: 20 machines and 100 jobs — size of the largest instance the scheduler was tested on
span.quote: We verified K = 3 was enough for even our largest testing JSSP, which has 20 machines and 100 jobs, because disjunctive graphs are densely connected.

span.label: 20 — episodes collected per PPO parameter update
span.quote: we set the number n of episodes per parameter update as 20 such that the PPO algorithm reliably estimates the state value and compute the gradient from it.
